title: Letters from Our Readers
paragraphs: Readers respond to E. Tammy Kim’s article about the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, Nicholas Lemann’s report about the Trump Administration’s attack on higher education, and Jill Lepore’s piece about whether A.I. needs a constitution. April 13, 2026 A Credit to Them E. Tammy Kim, in her article about the Consumer Financial Protection Bureau, captures something important that has gotten lost in the broader story of the Trump Administration’s dismantling of federal agencies: Russell Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget, isn’t merely stripping the C.F.P.B. of its enforcement power, he’s actively using it to benefit the industries it was created to police (“Pay Later,” March 16th). As a consumer-protection attorney who represents people in disputes against earned-wage-access fintech companies, I’d like to more fully examine a point that Kim touched on. On December 23rd, Vought’s bureau issued an advisory opinion concluding that certain earned-wage-access products are not considered “credit” under the Truth in Lending Act, the federal law that requires lenders to disclose costs and terms in a consistent manner to insure that consumers are able to understand what it is they’re signing up for and to compare products. It further determined that the fees such companies charge, which are, in practice, the way many of them make money, are not subject to those disclosure requirements. The opinion does not carry the force of law; it also runs against the recent current of federal-court decisions on the issue. Twelve courts have ruled, on motions to dismiss, that plaintiffs have sufficiently pleaded that these companies’ products constitute credit and that their accompanying fees are subject to the act’s protections. Five of the rulings came after the advisory opinion was published. Moreover, the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, one of the more consequential of the Court’s recent rulings, held that federal courts must exercise independent judgment on questions of statutory interpretation rather than deferring to agency readings of the law. Vought’s C.F.P.B. may be offering the industry reassurance, but the courts, it seems, are not deferring. Adrian Ward New York City Schooled Nicholas Lemann’s recent article details the Trump Administration’s attack on “élite” institutions over wokeness, D.E.I., antisemitism, transgender athletes, and hostility to conservative ideas in general (“Severance,” March 16th). The latest development in this relentless campaign is the Defense Department’s withdrawal of senior military leaders from academic programs at leading American universities. Each year, approximately a hundred senior officers from across all branches of the armed forces enroll in world-class courses of study at schools such as Harvard, Princeton, and Georgetown as part of the Senior Service College Fellows Program. These courses prepare senior servicepeople for positions of responsibility in the national-defense arena and also provide them with the opportunity to collaborate with their civilian counterparts, many of whom will go on to be leaders in a multitude of strategically important fields. But Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth has termed such civilian institutions “woke breeding grounds of toxic indoctrination,” and his visceral antipathy toward them will now preclude military leaders from gaining a broader understanding of national security. In 1901, Secretary of War Elihu Root founded the Army War College, and at its dedication, in 1908, he addressed the faculty and students: “Do not cease to be citizens of the United States. The conditions of Army life are such as to narrow your views. Strive to broaden your sympathies by mingling with those outside of the service and learning from them the things they can teach you. . . . Let our Army be never one of aggression but devoted to the interests of justice and peace.” That was true then, and it is especially true now. We need military leaders whose education benefits both the military profession and the enduring interests of the U.S. This latest ideological assault on professionalism advances neither objective. Peter V. Huisking Colonel, U.S. Army (Retired) Pasadena, Calif.
